articles.title: Child among eight killed by Israel on Gaza ‘ceasefire’ anniversary
articles.text:
Child among eight killed by Israel on Gaza ‘ceasefire’ anniversary | Israel-Palestine conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
People mourn Palestinians who were killed in an Israeli air attack in Gaza City, October 10, 2026 [Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
At least eight people, including an eight-year-old girl, have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to medical sources, a year after the United States-backed “ceasefire” came into effect – “in name only”.
Shahd Abdul-Razzaq al-Najjar, 8, was killed on Saturday by an Israeli quadcopter drone in the al-Jawazat area of western Gaza City, according to a source in ambulance and emergencies speaking to Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Israel kills or wounds Palestinian every 90 minutes in Gaza since ceasefire
list 2 of 3 Gaza ceasefire ‘exists in name only’, more than 100 NGOs say
list 3 of 3 A year after the ‘ceasefire’, Gaza’s healthcare is still collapsingend of list
In the same part of Gaza City, four people were killed and several injured in a separate Israeli bomb attack near Haider Abdel Shafi roundabout, the city’s al-Shifa Hospital said.
One more Palestinian was killed in an Israeli drone attack in the Tuffah neighbourhood of northeastern Gaza City, the hospital said.
One more person was killed in the northern Gaza Strip; and in the southern city of Khan Younis, a woman succumbed to injuries sustained in an Israeli attack earlier on Saturday.
People mourn loved ones killed in an Israeli air attack in Gaza City, October 10, 2026 [Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters]
Also on Saturday, the enclave’s Ministry of Health said at least 1,481 Palestinians have been killed and 5,254 injured since the so-called ceasefire came into effect on October 10 last year.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,370 people and injured 175, 371 since October 7, 2023, the ministry added.
In the past 24 hours, Israeli attacks killed at least nine people and injured 65, it said, adding that one more person succumbed to injuries sustained in previous Israeli aggression.
Advertisement
Al Jazeera’s Ibrahim al-Khalili, reporting from the site of a drone strike west of Gaza City on Saturday, said the attack underscores the continuing danger facing Palestinians living in the enclave despite the so-called “ceasefire”, reached on October 10, 2025.
“The ceasefire remains in place on paper, but on the ground, the threat to civilians has not gone away,” he said.
Reporting from Gaza’s Deir el-Balah, Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum said the “ceasefire” has only heightened uncertainty in the enclave.
“The rhythm of the genocide has not changed … it has fluctuated in intensity, but the danger has not gone away,” he said. “That’s why people believe that it has more consequences, far beyond the immediate loss of life.”
Ceasefire ‘in name only’
On Friday, more than 100 humanitarian, human rights and civil society organisations said in a joint statement that the ceasefire in Gaza exists only in name.
“The ceasefire exists in name only, with Israeli forces continuing to kill and injure Palestinians daily, and restrictions on aid, equipment and rebuilding materials preventing families from recovering,” the statement said.
In the occupied West Bank, at least 12 Israeli settler pogroms were recorded on Saturday morning, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
Israeli settlers assaulted Palestinian farmers through beatings, spraying them with pepper spray, stealing their property and attacking homes, the Wafa news agency reported. They also detained several Palestinians during the attacks with the help of the Israeli military forces.
In the Ramallah and el-Bireh Governorate, settlers, along with the army, forced farmers to leave their lands and threatened them against returning. Two farmers were beaten and pepper-sprayed, as settlers stole a vehicle and their phones.

articles.title: ‘How can you stop these kids?’ Indian capital on lockdown before protests
articles.text:
‘How can you stop these kids?’ Indian capital on lockdown before protests | Protests News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Police officers surrounded by yellow barricades direct commuters to an alternate route following road closures on the day of a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, on October 10, 2026 [Priyanshu Singh/Reuters]
By Yashraj Sharma
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
New Delhi, India – Heavy police barricades line the streets around Connaught Place, the colonial-era square near Jantar Mantar, on Saturday morning as police have begun detaining groups of protesters arriving for planned demonstrations.
They are here in support of the influential Gen-Z movement and Cockroach Janta Party, which have called for the resignation of India’s election chief, amid a bitter dispute over who gets to vote in the world’s most populous democracy.
Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and a rollback of a controversial voter revision exercise which has struck 130 million names from the voter list.
For now, an eerie silence hangs over parts of central New Delhi. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has gone to lengths to turn the city into a fortress, deploying nearly 30,000 personnel onto the streets.
Police ⁠have also detained the founder of ⁠the Cockroach Janta Party, Abhijeet Dipke.
Indian TV channels reported early on Saturday that officers met Dipke at New Delhi airport ⁠after he arrived ⁠from the financial capital Mumbai and asked him to call ⁠off the protest as authorities ⁠had banned it.
CJP leaders ⁠Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained from their flight ‌upon landing, the movement said in a statement.
On Friday, the government extraordinarily cancelled all trains to New Delhi; locked down more than 50 metro stations; imposed an internet shutdown; and sent personnel to thousands of students in local communities to warn them against participation in the protest.
Advertisement
Several students en route to New Delhi from different states of India were dragged out of trains and buses and detained by the police. Many have been placed under house arrest in cities hundreds of kilometres away from New Delhi.
The Cockroach movement says thousands have been detained across India as Modi’s government intensifies its crackdown. Yet undeterred protesters have pledged to keep returning to the streets.
‘Made EMERGENCY official’
Current restrictions in the Indian capital and the nationwide crackdown on protesters have evoked memories of the 1975 Emergency, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties, censored the press and jailed political opponents.
“Narendra Modi just made EMERGENCY official,” Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, wrote in a post on X. “This intimidation is not going to work, Modi. The youth of this country are no longer scared of you.”
Neha Bora, the firebrand Gen-Z protest leader and the national president of the left student body All India Students’ Association, equated the Modi government with British colonialist forces that unsuccessfully clamped down on India’s independence movement. She called on the masses to join the protest.
On Saturday morning, young people were trying to respond to her call despite the police restrictions in place.
Santosh Kumar, 29, a street sweeper in the outer circle of Connaught Place, told Al Jazeera he feels frustrated seeing teenagers detained at police barricades.
“How can you stop these kids? They are detaining 10; 50 more are coming. Modi, the dictator’s time is up: He will not even stay until 2029 (the time of the next elections).
“This is the time we turn Delhi into Nepal and Bangladesh – learn from them and take back our country,” he said, referring to youth-led movements in those countries.
Sameer Irshad, 28, an engineer from Gurugram, approached the barricades near Connaught Place while pushing his 57-year-old mother Sheeba Abdi in a wheelchair.
Abdi told us: “This sort of crackdown, where we cannot peacefully express our dissent, is unseen in Delhi. Why has government turned this place into a fortress? Why are they so scared of citizens like me?”
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters sleep in a park next to the site of Saturday’s planned protest seeking the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026 [Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters]
Under house arrest
Last month, India was shaken by revelations of divisions within the supposedly autonomous body that is in charge of conducting elections, over controversial policies that critics say have disenfranchised tens of millions of people.
Advertisement
India’s Election Commission chief, Gyanesh Kumar, was accused of overruling concerns raised by the two other election commissioners about the integrity of ongoing changes in the voter database, an investigation by The Indian Express reported.
India is among the few countries to have taken an active approach to enrolling every last voter.
Critics say the ongoing revision of the voter list flips the foundational principle of Indian democracy: Demanding that citizens prove their voting rights, and disproportionately targeting Muslims, economically weaker sections, minorities and other vulnerable groups in Indian society.
Arif, a 24-year-old district coordinator for the Students’ Federation of India, another left-wing student organisation to have joined the protest call, was locked in his home in Saharanpur, nearly 200km (125 miles) from New Delhi, on Thursday.
“Several police officials started beating my door out of nowhere late at night, asking my parents for details of my whereabouts,” Arif, who did not want to give his full name, told Al Jazeera from his home in Saharanpur, where he is currently detained under the police’s watch around the clock.

articles.title: Suspect killed after 13 kindergarteners taken hostage, beaten in Brazil
articles.text:
Suspect killed after 13 kindergarteners taken hostage, beaten in Brazil | Crime News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Brazil police rescue 13 children taken hostage at kindergarten
By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and The Associated Press
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
Brazilian police have rescued 13 children who had been taken hostage at a kindergarten in the southern city of Curitiba after killing the suspect, who threatened to set fire to the building, according to officials.
At least one of the children was wounded in Friday’s incident, the commander of the military police special forces unit in Parana state, Alexandre Lopes Dias, told reporters without elaborating on who or what injured the child.
Parana police spokesperson Leticia Martins told journalists outside the kindergarten that the suspect jumped the gate on Friday, broke into a classroom and held 13 children hostage.
He then spread a flammable substance in the room and held a lighter in his hand. He was carrying a knife and also what was initially believed to be a firearm, but later was found to be fake.
“Our negotiating teams were in place but saw no alternative but to neutralise him,” said Martins, who did not specify whether the suspect had expressed a specific reason for his actions.
[Al Jazeera]
The incident took place in the neighbourhood of Sao Braz in Curitiba, a city of 1.8 million residents located 400km (250 miles) south of Sao Paulo.
Lopes Dias told reporters the suspect was identified as a man who suffered from schizophrenia, but he did not reveal the man’s identity or how he was killed.
“During the entire negotiation, he stayed with all the children around him and one on his lap,” the police official said.
Children beaten
Talks lasted up to three hours. The children became agitated, and the attacker started hitting them, Lopes Dias told reporters.
Advertisement
“Once we realised that the kids were becoming increasingly upset and that the attacker started assaulting them physically, we opted for a tactical intervention to avoid a greater problem,” he explained.
Local media showed footage of tearful parents outside the school waiting for information as the negotiations between the suspect and police were ongoing. Minutes after what local media described as flash bangs, officers emerged carrying some of the children outside.
“We entered the classroom using a very tactical approach with little risk for the children,” Lopes Dias added.
Curitiba Mayor Eduardo Pimentel wrote on Instagram: “The 13 children are alive and safe! After anguishing and tense moments, this is the news we were all waiting for.”
Brazil in recent years has experienced multiple attacks on schools. In April 2023, a man killed four children with an axe at a day care in Blumenau, also in southern Brazil.
Curitiba City Hall said in a statement that the children and school staffers would receive psychological support.

articles.title: Journalist Hamurabi Huesca Manzano killed in Mexico’s Oaxaca
articles.text:
Journalist Hamurabi Huesca Manzano killed in Mexico’s Oaxaca | Gun Violence News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Hamurabi Huesca Manzano is the ninth journalist killed in Mexico this year [Fausto Camacho/AP]
By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
A journalist moonlighting as a taxi driver has been shot dead in the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca, the ninth killed in the country this year, according to human rights organisation Article 19.
Hamurabi Huesca Manzano, who owned the news website Pinotepa Comunica, was killed on Friday after an armed group opened fire on him and two others, according to the state prosecutor’s report.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Search continues for kidnapped Mexican journalist Roxana Guzman
list 2 of 3 Journalist killed in Mexico after years of exposing corruption
list 3 of 3 Mexican influencer shot dead during livestreamend of list
The office said one line of inquiry suggests that a dispute happened between local criminal groups, and that the intended target of the shooting was a man known as “El Dario”.
El Dario, infamous for instigating violence on the Oaxaca coast, was wounded in the shooting and died in hospital hours later. According to prosecutors, Huesca Manzano was working as a taxi driver, waiting to take El Dario somewhere else when the journalist was shot dead.
The prosecutor’s office says the attackers have been “fully identified”, but did not name them or say whether Huesca Manzano’s journalistic work played any role.
Local reports give differing accounts of where the attack happened, as well; a number of them say Huesca Manzano was shot at his home and that a woman was also injured.
Article 19 condemned the killing and said on X: “We demand that the prosecutor’s office treat his journalistic work as a priority in its investigation.”
The mayor of San Miguel Tlacamama, Antonio Olmedo Mendoza, confirmed Manzano’s death and offered condolences in a statement, local media reported.
“With deep sorrow, I regret the passing of Hamurabi Sinclair Huesca Manzano,” he said, adding that he joined the grief of his family, friends and colleagues.
Advertisement
Mexico is notorious for being one of the most dangerous countries for journalists, with more than 150 media workers killed there since 1994, according to Reporters Without Borders.

articles.title: Israel’s economy prospers despite years of war, but prices worry voters
articles.text:
Israel’s economy prospers despite years of war, but prices worry voters | Israel Election 2026 News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
High-rise buildings are seen near a beach in Tel Aviv, Israel, on June 16, 2019 [Amir Cohen/Reuters]
By John Power
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
After three years of Israel’s multi-front war in the Middle East, it would be no surprise if this month’s Knesset elections were taking place against the backdrop of an economy in dire straits.
Instead, Israel’s economy is – by many measures – flourishing.
After slowing sharply in the initial aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel has rebounded to become one of the fastest-growing advanced economies in recent years.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025, picking up from a 1 percent expansion in 2024, and 3.2 percent in the first half of this year, according to government figures.
The Bank of Israel has forecast 4 percent growth for the whole of 2026 and 5.5 percent growth in 2027 – projections that far exceed the outlooks for major economies such as the United States, United Kingdom, France, Canada, and Japan.
Over the past three years, the shekel has strengthened against the US dollar, hitting a three-decade high in May, and Israel’s stock market has surged, with the benchmark TA-125 up more than 110 percent.
Meanwhile, unemployment stands at 2.8 percent, while inflation is modest at 1.5 percent.
Against this relatively rosy economic backdrop, campaigning for the October 27 election has been dominated by national security, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, and retired general Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar, each claiming to be most qualified to keep Israelis safe.
An election advertisement is seen in Ramat Gan, Israel on September 23, 2026 [Jack Guez/AFP]
Driving Israel’s striking economic resilience has been a booming tech sector largely insulated from its conflicts spanning Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran and Yemen.
Advertisement
Despite being on a war footing since October 2023, Israel has attracted record levels of investment in tech, the driver of about one-fifth of economic activity, amid the frenetic global rollout of artificial intelligence (AI).
Total direct foreign investment hit a record $26.2bn last year, up 78 percent from 2024, led by US tech giants Alphabet and Palo Alto Networks’ record-breaking acquisitions of Israeli cybersecurity firms Wiz and CyberArk, respectively.
Foreign capital has continued to flood into the country this year, with inflows reaching a quarterly record of $14.1bn in the January-March period, according to government figures.
Along with prospering from the global AI boom, Israel’s tech scene has benefitted from its close ties to the local defence sector, which has ramped up orders from hundreds of startups supplying everything from radar systems to communications platforms and anti-drone technology.
While Israel’s economy has bounced back in part due to robust employment and wage growth, its resilience is primarily an “export-driven story that reflects strong global technology demand, particularly in areas where Israel – and multinational firms operating from Israel – is globally competitive, such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence,” said Keren Uziyel, a senior analyst for the Middle East and Africa at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU).
“Interest in Israel’s technology goods and services is driving high levels of FDI and venture capital fundraising, and boosting the capital markets, which in turn is having significant wealth effects and boosting government revenue,” Uziyel told Al Jazeera.
People walk near high-rise buildings in the high-tech business area of Tel Aviv, Israel May 15, 2017 [Amir Cohen/Reuters]
But Israel’s military campaigns have come at an enormous cost to the public purse.
In March, the Bank of Israel estimated that Israel’s war costs to date had reached approximately 350 billion shekels ($114.6bn) – a figure not including the then recently-launched Iran war.
Military expenditures are on track to rise substantially in the coming years as Israeli leaders double down on “national security”.
Netanyahu, whose right-wing coalition has cast security as “the foundation of everything else”, has pushed to raise the annual defence budget to 183 billion shekels ($60bn), equivalent to roughly 9 percent of GDP.
If passed, the budget would raise military spending by two and a half times what it was before October 7.
Outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid has backed an expanded defence budget, but has clashed with Netanyahu about how to fund it.
Advertisement
Economic concerns
Though security has dominated the run-up to the election, opinion polling suggests that Israelis also view the economy as a key concern.
In an opinion poll released by the Israel Democracy Institute last month, 38 percent of Jewish Israelis and 46 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up about 20 percent of the population – chose the economy and the cost of living as the most important or second-most important election issue.
Israel’s high cost of living, in particular, has long been a source of public discontent.
Israel has for years ranked among the most expensive countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a dynamic economists attribute to the country’s limited trade relations with its neighbours and cumbersome regulations.
Though Israel’s overall rate of inflation has been modest, food prices have risen at a faster pace, increasing 8 percent between the start of 2024 and mid-2026, according to consumer advocacy group Lobby 99.
“People are worried about the economy but not so much about the macroeconomic situation, more so on their personal perspectives, especially cost of living,” Ayal Kimhi, vice president of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research in Tel Aviv, told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Russia kills 15 in Ukraine as US hosts ‘productive’ talks to end war
articles.text:
Russia kills 15 in Ukraine as US hosts ‘productive’ talks to end war | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Rescue workers carry a body after pulling it from the rubble of a residential building destroyed by a Russian air attack in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, October 10, 2026 [Kateryna Klochko/AP]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
Russian air attacks on Ukraine have killed at least 15 people in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, according to the Ukrainian prosecutor’s office.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier on Saturday that three people were among those killed in the Russian attacks on the city.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Ukraine pushes Russia back in Donetsk as military, civilian casualties soar
list 2 of 3 Trump announces Russian diesel deal amid soaring US fuel prices
list 3 of 3 Putin tells Trump peace talks are unlikely, cites Ukraine drone attacksend of list
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rescuers continued searching for people under the rubble, he said.
Speaking from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said “there are more and more daytime attacks taking place across Ukraine, for example a glide bomb hit a bus stop earlier in the week, killing 30 people, and in Kyiv recently more and more jet-powered drones are striking targets during the daytime.
“One video that was released recently shows a man standing in front of a school and running from a building when he heard the jet approaching, surviving only by a few seconds – all of this underscores just how dangerous things have become for civilians here in Ukraine lately,” MacAlpine said.
US, Ukraine, EU meeting
The attacks come a day after US, Ukrainian, and European officials met in Miami, Florida, to discuss a proposal for ⁠ending the Russia-Ukraine war, US envoy Steve Witkoff said in a statement posted to X.
Witkoff said on Friday that “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace”.
Advertisement
Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO”.
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict”, Witkoff said.
He also noted the “productive” talks discussed “Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession”.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday the conflict had reached a dangerous “stalemate”, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
“The other way that stalemates end is through escalation,” Rubio told reporters, warning that the conflict could spread to neighbouring NATO countries.
Advertisement

articles.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of military-linked Myanmar businessman
articles.text:
US lifts sanctions on daughter of military-linked Myanmar businessman | Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
The entrance to the US Treasury Department [File: Ken Cedeno/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters
Published On 10 Oct 202610 Oct 2026
The United States has removed sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the military-installed government.
The US Department of the Treasury removed Theint Win Htet from its sanctions list on Friday, according to its website, after she sued them in July.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 ‘They are crying’: Refugees in Malaysia in fear amid Myanmar deportation
list 2 of 3 What would justice look like if there were no Rohingya left in Myanmar?
list 3 of 3 Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing visits Malaysia amid concerns over repatriationsend of list
The decision followed a Reuters news agency report that said US President Donald Trump’s administration has opened talks with Myanmar’s government, a break from years of US policy that sanctioned the generals responsible for a coup in 2021 against Myanmar’s democratically elected government.
In January 2024, the Treasury Department under former President Joe Biden’s administration targeted the Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies, which was founded by Theint Win Htet’s father, Thein Win Zaw, along with his family.
The department said the company supplied fuel to the military and owned at least 20 firms with close ties to the military leadership.
Theint Win Htet originally requested her removal in a lawsuit filed against the Biden administration. That case was dismissed last year. She then filed a second complaint in July, arguing that she has no role in her father’s business.
The sanctions had blocked her US credit cards, restricted her foreign bank accounts and forced her to abandon her master’s degree at Columbia University in New York. She now lives in Thailand with her mother, who was taken off the US sanctions list last year.
Theint Win Htet’s lawyer, Washington, DC-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the federal court in the US capital on Friday to voluntarily dismiss the lawsuit after her delisting.
Advertisement
‘Deplorable’
The group Justice For Myanmar has condemned the Treasury Department’s decision, saying Myanmar’s military is escalating attacks on civilians.
“It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta’s terror,” the ‌group ‌said.
The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military officers and companies after the 2021 coup, which sparked a civil war that has killed about 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
Washington lifted sanctions in July last year on several other Myanmar nationals and a company accused of aiding the military.
Advertisement
